Personal identity is not the persistence of a body or an organism but the persistence of a mind, and the most defensible account of what that persistence consists in traces back to Locke's insight that a person is constituted by the continuity of consciousness and receives its most rigorous elaboration in Parfit's work on psychological continuity. What makes some future person me is not that they share my flesh, my cells, or even my brain matter considered as biological tissue, but that they stand in the right relations of memory, personality, and intention to my present self. Locke saw that if consciousness could be transferred, identity would follow it; Parfit refined this by observing that memory and other psychological connections come in degrees and form overlapping chains, so that identity over time is secured not by any single direct link but by a continuous chain of psychological connectedness. The clearest vindication of this view lies in the brain-transplant thought experiment: if my brain were placed in another body while my original body were given a different brain, virtually everyone judges that I go with the brain. But the brain matters here only because it carries my psychology; it is the vehicle, not the ground, of my persistence. Were psychology preservable by some other means, our verdict would track it there as well. The physical substrate is significant only instrumentally, as the current carrier of what actually matters.

The biological continuity view, which locates identity in the persistence of the human organism, cannot account for why identity matters to us in the ways it manifestly does. Prudential concern for one's future — the reason I save for retirement, undergo painful medical treatment now for later benefit, or fear my own death — is intelligible only if the future person who reaps the benefit or suffers the loss is psychologically continuous with me. If a human organism persists in an irreversible vegetative state, with all higher cortical function permanently destroyed, biological continuity is fully preserved: the same organism breathes, metabolizes, and lives on. Yet almost no one thinks that anticipating this condition is anything like anticipating one's own future experiences, precisely because there will be no experiences and no psychological connections to the person who once inhabited that body. The same holds for moral responsibility: we hold a person accountable for past actions because they remember doing them, endorse or repudiate the intentions behind them, and are shaped by the character that produced them. A body that has lost all psychological connection to its earlier deeds is not a fitting subject of praise or blame for those deeds, however continuous its cells. The normative work that identity performs — grounding rational self-concern and moral responsibility — is done by psychological relations, and where those relations vanish while biology persists, the normative weight vanishes with them.

Parfit's reductionism, which holds that personal identity consists in nothing over and above psychological continuity and connectedness, is preferable to non-reductionist accounts that posit some further fact — a soul, a Cartesian ego, or a bare metaphysical simple — because it dissolves rather than deepens the puzzles that identity generates. Consider fission: if my brain's hemispheres were separated and each transplanted into a viable body, both resulting persons would be psychologically continuous with me. A non-reductionist must insist on a determinate answer to whether I am one, the other, both, or neither, and every available verdict is arbitrary: nothing in the case favors the left over the right, and identity cannot as a matter of logic be one-many. The reductionist simply notes that identity is not what matters; what matters is psychological continuity, and that relation obtains, doubled, in both descendants. The puzzle disappears once we stop treating identity as a further fact demanding a further answer. The same virtue appears in cases of gradual psychological replacement, where one's memories, values, and traits are slowly exchanged for another's. Non-reductionists must locate a sharp threshold at which identity is lost, but no principled threshold exists; reductionism recognizes that identity, like the continuity that constitutes it, admits of degrees and vague boundaries, and that our practical concerns can be calibrated to the underlying gradations without demanding an all-or-nothing verdict the facts do not supply. By treating identity as constituted by psychological relations rather than as a separately existing fact riding atop them, reductionism yields determinate practical guidance exactly where non-reductionism produces mystery.
